e.meaning: from the Maasai people of East Africa
e.etymology: Taken from the Maasai, also spelled Masai, the cattle-herding people of Kenya and Tanzania. Their name means speakers of the Maa language.

assoc.t: the Maasai people of Kenya and Tanzania

e.etymology: From the surname taken from Kendal, a town in Cumbria, England, whose name means valley of the river Kent. Kendall is the more common spelling for the given name.

assoc.t: Kendall Jenner, model and reality TV star (spelled Kendall)
Kendal, market town by England's Lake District

e.etymology: From azalia, an older spelling of azalea, the flowering shrub. Its botanical name comes from Greek azaleos, 'dry', for the dry soil the plant was thought to prefer.
The Italian form of George, from Latin Georgius and Greek Georgios, from georgos, 'farmer', literally 'earth-worker'. The name spread through devotion to Saint George.
namesakes: Giorgio Moroder (disco and film music producer)

assoc.t: Giorgio Armani fashion house
Giorgio Beverly Hills perfume

e.etymology: A Japanese girls' name most often written with the characters for ai, 'love', and ko, 'child'; other spellings use ai meaning 'indigo' or 'together'. Japan's Princess Aiko carries the love spelling.

assoc.t: Jhene Aiko, R&B singer (Aiko is her middle name)

e.etymology: From Arabic saniyya, 'brilliant, exalted'. Among Tatar and Bashkir families the same spelling comes from Arabic thaniya, 'second', a name for a second daughter.
A region named in Luke 3:1 after its chief town Abila, probably from Hebrew abel, 'meadow'. Abilene, Kansas took the Biblical name, and Abilene, Texas was named for the Kansas town.

assoc.t: Abilene, city in West Texas
Abilene, Kansas, Eisenhower's boyhood hometown
Abilene, 1963 country hit by George Hamilton IV

e.etymology: The Arabic form of Aaron, from Hebrew Aharon, whose meaning is unknown and may be Egyptian. In the Quran, Harun is a prophet and the brother of Musa (Moses).
From the English color word, from Old French bleu. Long a nickname and a middle name, as in Bonnie Blue, it rose as a first name after Beyonce and Jay-Z named their daughter Blue Ivy in 2012.
namesakes: Blue Ivy Carter (daughter of Beyonce and Jay-Z)

assoc.t: Blue, the puppy of Nickelodeon's Blue's Clues
blue, everyday word for feeling sad
Blue, the trained raptor in Jurassic World
Blue Ivy Carter, daughter of Beyoncé and Jay-Z

e.note: Blue also means sad, and it is a common name for dogs.

e.etymology: A modern American variation on Xavier, with the -en ending of names like Jayden and Damien. Xavier itself comes from a Basque place name meaning new house.
A recent name with no single source: an elaboration of Cali or Calla, or a C- spelling of Kalia, in the style of Talia and Dalia.
A modern American name built on the Ry- of Rylee and Rylan with a feminine -a ending, in the pattern of Kyla, Myla and Nyla.
A medieval Spanish royal name, probably of Gothic origin and debated meaning. It spread across Europe after Mozart used it for Donna Elvira in Don Giovanni (1787).

assoc.t: Elvira, Mistress of the Dark, campy horror hostess
Elvira, 1981 country hit by the Oak Ridge Boys
Donna Elvira in Mozart's Don Giovanni
Elvira Hancock, Michelle Pfeiffer's role in Scarface

e.note: Many Americans first think of Elvira, Mistress of the Dark, the vampy TV horror hostess.

e.etymology: From an English surname for a Briton or, more often in medieval England, a Breton who had come over from Brittany.
An American blend of Jay with the -lyn ending, one of many spellings of Jaylen and Jaylin that spread in the 1990s and 2000s.
The Portuguese and Spanish form of Ronald, which comes through Scottish Gaelic from Old Norse Rognvaldr: rogn, 'counsel', plus valdr, 'power, ruler'. Soccer made it famous worldwide.

assoc.t: Cristiano Ronaldo, Portuguese soccer superstar

e.etymology: A spelling of Christopher used mostly in Spanish-speaking families, where it sits beside the older Spanish form Cristobal. From Greek Khristophoros: Khristos, 'Christ', plus pherein, 'to carry'.
A phonetic American respelling of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, the rhetorical question 'who is like God?' and the name of the archangel.
An American spelling of Maren or Marin, names that go back to Latin Marinus, 'of the sea'. Maren is the Danish and Norwegian form of Marina; Maryn is also a Polish men's name from the same root.

e.meaning: portion, a part of the whole
e.etymology: From Sanskrit amsha, 'portion, share', often understood as a part of the divine. It has been a popular boys' name in India since the 2000s.
From the English word, which comes through Old French from Latin aeternitas. It is a modern American word name in the family of Destiny, Serenity and Trinity.

assoc.t: Eternity, Calvin Klein fragrance

e.etymology: A respelling of Arabella that brings out the nickname Ari. Arabella has been used in Scotland since the Middle Ages; it may come from Latin orabilis, 'yielding to prayer', or be a variant of Annabel.
A short form of India, Indiana or Indigo used as a name in its own right. The spelling Indie is equally common.

assoc.t: indie, short for independent music and film
Indy, nickname of Indiana Jones
Indy, short for the Indianapolis 500

e.etymology: From the Irish surname O Raighne, 'descendant of Raighne', a Gaelic form of the Old Norse name Rognvaldr. As a girls' name it is also heard as a softer take on Rain.
e.note: Sounds exactly like the word rainy.

e.etymology: From a surname for someone who lived by a holt, the Old English word for a copse or small wood. The same word and surname are found in Dutch, German and Scandinavian.

assoc.t: Captain Raymond Holt of Brooklyn Nine-Nine
Henry Holt, book and textbook publisher

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Zachary, the English form of Hebrew Zekharyah, 'Yahweh remembers', the name of an Old Testament prophet and of the father of John the Baptist.
A 20th-century coinage, apparently Tara combined with names like Karen. Actor Tyrone Power gave it to his daughter Taryn in 1953, echoing his own name, and it caught on from there.
namesakes: Taryn Manning (Orange Is the New Black actress)

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Latin Fidelis, from fidelis, 'faithful', a name borne by several saints.
namesakes: Fidel Castro (Cuban revolutionary and longtime leader)

assoc.t: Fidel Castro, Cuba's communist leader for five decades

e.note: For most Americans the name points straight to Fidel Castro.

e.etymology: One of the Puritan virtue names, from the English word prudence, Latin prudentia, 'foresight, good judgment'. It continues the medieval name Prudentia.
namesakes: Prudence Halliwell (Prue, the eldest sister on Charmed)

assoc.t: Dear Prudence, the Beatles song
Dear Prudence, Slate's advice column

e.note: Close to the word prude, which can invite teasing.

e.etymology: A modern American name of uncertain source, close in sound to Kellen, Callan and Galen and to Jalen, which rose in the same years.
From Latin mirabilis, 'wonderful, marvelous'. Mirabel was a medieval English and French name; mirabelle is also the French word for a small golden plum.

assoc.t: Mirabel Madrigal, heroine of Disney's Encanto
mirabelle, a small golden French plum
